items.title: Flip Phillips interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 11, 1996
items.q: We had a good rhythm section there. Jo Jones, Hank Jones, Ray Brown.

ctx.x: Well they did record one particular night, where you played the solo on “Perdido” which has followed you around.

Yeah that was a good one. That came off, we had a concert at, not the Island, the Mosque Theater in Newark at eight o’clock, and at twelve o’clock we went to Carnegie Hall in New York, and that’s when it was made, in 1947. We played it and everybody was relaxed and it just came off. It was wonderful you know at the time, and we didn’t think anything of it. And then when the record — all the disc jockeys started playing it. And it was quite a thing. It sold a million albums. For an instrumental, that’s great. And…
How can you go wrong with those guys behind you?

items.title: Ray Brown interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, AZ, April 16, 2000
items.q: I remember we would finish a tour and it would be, we’d go in the studio and it would be Coleman Hawkins, Lester Young, Ben Webster, Flip Phillips, Illinois Jacquet, Johnny Hodges, Charlie Parker, Dizzy and Roy and maybe Charlie Shavers and Oscar Peterson and Barney Kessell or Herb Ellis and myself

ctx.x: Norman Granz was a pretty important figure in jazz during those years. Was he a pretty upright guy to work for?

Oh yeah. You know he did a lot of brilliant things. First of all he put jazz into the concert hall. He took it out of the dance hall and put it in the concert hall. He took it out of the night club and put it in the concert hall. He gave people the very best musicians, I mean he got the top people, he always had top people playing for him, and he paid top salaries. I mean he was a tough guy. I remember we would finish a tour and it would be, we’d go in the studio and it would be Coleman Hawkins, Lester Young, Ben…
